newsitem.title: POLAND: OPINION- Polish NOBE macroeconomic forecast.
newsitem.headline: OPINION- Polish NOBE macroeconomic forecast.

text.p: NOBE Independent Centre for Economic Studies
Quarterly forecasts of the economic development of Poland

The Polish economy was growing by more than 7 percent during the last two quarters. However, the fast growth was accompanied by a rapid deterioration of the current account balance and the growing trade deficit. The level of the current account deficit is still acceptable but the negative trend should be stopped over the next 6-12 months to avoid more serious economic perturbations. The growth of domestic credit and consumption should be slowed down to stabilise the curent account deficit at the level below four percent of GDP. In our view no drastic policy measures are necessary to achieve this target. However, some policy moves are unavoidable and likely to take place despite the coming general elections.
Four main factors influenced the economic performance of Poland in the first quarter of 1997.

Firstly, the dynamics of domestic consumption remained very high both due to a fast growth of wages and consumer credit as well as because of the continuing investment boom. Total growth of domestic consumption exceeded 11 percent compared to the same period year ago.
Secondly, the rapid growth was accompanied by even faster increase in imports (above 20 percent), in a large part due to purchases of capital goods.

Thirdly, the growth rates of exports started to pick up slowly. Nevertheless, as the dynamics of imports remained still significantly higher than the dynamics of exports, the external balance deteriorated considerably. The balance of payments trade deficit increased during the last six months by almost $6 billion and the current account deficit by $2.5 billion.
Fourthly, inflationary pressure kept falling despite the fast demand growth and a relatively expansionary monetary policy.

The observed growth pattern is not sustainable over the longer period. The deterioration of the external balance has not reached dangerous levels yet, could cause problems 4-5 quarters from now if it countinues to worsen. However, we are relatively optimistic, as there are reasons to believe that the situation may improve without drastic policy measures.

1. The trade deficit is growing rapidly, but its level is still acceptable. A trade deficit is a normal phenomenon in a fast growing economy importing foreign capital. The current account deficit was about one percent of GDP in 1996 and is likely to grow to 3.5-3.8 percent in 1997. This is still a level that can be comfortably financed by capital inflows.

However, any further deterioration in 1998 may be dangerous. That means, that although Poland has got some room for manoeuvre to accomodate the unavoidable deterioration of the external account in 1997, the trend of the rapid deterioration should be stopped over the next four quarters.

2. We expect some improvement in exports to take place mainly due to the faster growth in Western Europe and despite the weak German Mark. Such an improvement will not be enough to restore the external equilibrium of Poland, but may help to curb the growth of the deficit.

3. Under these circumstances current growth rates of investment and consumer demand (over 20 percent and almost 8 percent respectively) are not sustainable over the longer period. Our assessment is that the growth of investment should gradually cool down to 12-15 percent over the next four quarters and the growth of consumption to about five percent.

4. No drastic policy measures are necessary or desirable to achieve this target. Monetary policy is the key here. As growth of domestic credit should be curbed, there is no room for interest rate cuts. To the contrary, NBP may slightly increase the basic rates in the coming months, or continue using other instruments that increase the price of money. Probably no one-off devaluation will be necessary, and the crawling peg will continue at its present rate of one percent a month.

The crawl is unlikely to be be cut below 0.9-1 percent a month over the next four quarters. Finally, as the budget deficit is still under control, we do not see reasons for fiscal adjustment. With a slowdown in GDP growth, and low inflation, the budget may find itself under some pressure in the second half of 1997. The deficit, even if the target is exceeded, should not reach three percent of GDP.

As the outcome of current trends and policy changes we expect the growth rate of domestic consumption to slow down to seven percent in the last quarter of 1997 on lower investment growth and lower private consumption.

The growth rate of exports is not likely to exceed that of imports before 1998. GDP growth will fall to about five percent in the last quarter of 1997. The annual growth rate in 1997 will be about six percent, very similar to GDP growth in 1996. GDP growth may start picking up only after the trend of current account deterioration is stopped. Table 2 shows projected inflationary developments in the next four quarters. Weakening indexation mechainsms, more rigid monetary policy, and possible slow growth of food prices will result in the continuous slowdown of consumer prices. The process of the general fall of inflationary expectations may be significantly disrupted if devaluation expectations due to the lack of a transparent exchange rate policy.

Producer price growth will stabilize around 11 percent. The fall of PPI will resume in 1998 (to a one-digit level) after the crawling peg devaluation of the zloty is slowed down below 0.9 percent in a month.
